facts.text: During 2023 about 35 million people in sub-Saharan Africa were newly connected to electricity. Because the population rose by 30 million that year, the number lacking electricity dropped by just 5 million, from 570 million to 565 million.
In 2023, sub-Saharan Africa was home to 85% of the world’s people without electricity, up from 50% in 2010.
Central and Southern Asia cut the number of people without electricity from 414 million in 2010 to 27 million in 2023.
Worldwide, 92% of people had electricity in 2023, and 666 million people still did not.
In 2023, 84% of the people without electricity lived in rural areas. Most live in remote, low-income or conflict-affected places where the grid is hard to extend.
From 2020 to 2022, 55% of new connections in sub-Saharan Africa came from decentralized renewable energy, for example solar home systems and small solar grids.
Kenya was among the fastest-electrifying countries between 2010 and 2023, reaching 76% access by 2023.
Nigeria had the largest electricity access gap in the world in 2023, with 86.6 million people lacking electricity.
Mini-grid projects in Nigeria have connected nearly 6 million people.
Kenya’s Last Mile Connectivity Program aims to connect every household within 600 meters of a transformer.
Under the program the household connection fee was cut from 35,000 Kenyan shillings (US$343) to 15,000 shillings (US$147), payable in installments; each connection costs the utility about US$1,000.

Kenya is the birthplace of pay-as-you-go solar, in which customers pay for a solar home system in small installments, often by mobile money. The Kenyan company M-KOPA first sold it commercially in 2012.
Pay-as-you-go systems are switched off if the customer stops paying; it is a lease-to-own model, so customers end up owning the system.
Pay-as-you-go models made up 39% of off-grid solar sales in 2023, up from 24% in 2018.
Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda, which have made fast progress on electricity access, combine extending the grid with decentralized renewable options such as off-grid solar.
Mission 300, led by the World Bank and the African Development Bank, aims to bring electricity to 300 million people in Africa by 2030.
